source.title: Counterfactual Memorization in Neural Language Models
source.authors: Chiyuan Zhang; Daphne Ippolito; Katherine Lee; Matthew Jagielski; Florian Tramèr; Nicholas Carlini

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. The header identifies arXiv:2112.12938v2 (13 Oct 2023), and the paper text states 37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2023), differing from the supplied year 2021.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies counterfactual memorization and influence in language models. It does not test any listed version about generalization gaps, and its memorization measure is distinct from the behaviors those versions name.
record.gate_note: The reported language-model measurements concern per-example counterfactual memorization and influence, not the listed generalization-gap versions. Those measurements are recorded under fits_no_version. Results from cited prior work are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures document-level counterfactual memorization and influence in language models. It does not compare removal of highly memorized examples against equal-sized random removals and retrained aggregate test accuracy, as V8 requires. It also performs none of the interventions or comparisons required by V1–V7. Borrowing V8's source's estimation framework does not test or rely on its removal finding.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors find rare counterfactually memorized documents in three text corpora, an inverse association with duplication, and strong influence of some memorized documents on predictions for related validation and generated texts. Grover supplies generated texts; the study does not directly measure counterfactual changes in Grover's generation behavior.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains language models on random dataset subsets and estimates per-example counterfactual memorization and influence; it does not use the interventions or measures in the listed claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and training epoch affect the reported memorization profiles; the authors report more memorization with more epochs and broadly consistent distribution shapes across the three datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: Counterfactually memorized documents occur in all three corpora; individual training documents can strongly influence predictions on related validation or generated texts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Including particular training documents can substantially raise language-model per-token accuracy on those documents and on related held-out texts.

fits_no_version.finding: Counterfactual memorization increases with training duration and correlates negatively with near-duplicate counts among duplicated RealNews documents.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Document-level counterfactual memorization depends on training duration and duplication.

record.peer_reviewed: Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2023), as stated in the paper text
record.problems: The authors state that the models and datasets are much smaller than modern standards, the study focuses mainly on English, and training dynamics were only preliminarily investigated. Accuracy and memorization figures are aggregates or plots without reported uncertainty in the cited results.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows were created for illustrative training/validation or training/generation example pairs in Tables 2 and 3; they are individual examples, not separately reported aggregate outcomes bearing on a listed version. Figure-only histograms are recorded as distribution-level rows rather than reconstructing point values.

untested.parts: Fixed random-label fitting and held-out performance under natural versus random labels.
Width-dependent test error beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer generalization under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout's effect on held-out error across training-set sizes and regularization settings.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps, and comparison with alternative measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples, and comparing aggregate held-out accuracy.

record.verdict_notes: A generalization gap or a memorization–influence association alone does not test any listed version. No version-specific verdict is warranted.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out accuracy on natural versus random labels.
Width sweeps and test error beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and architectural bias.
Dropout and weight-decay effects on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to the training-test gap.
Removing the most memorized examples and comparing retrained test accuracy with random removals.

rows.subject: Transformer-based language models equivalent to (decoder only) T5-base
rows.operation_detail: Compared per-token accuracy on examples in the training set between models trained with the example (IN) and without it (OUT).

conditions.value: counterfactual memorization: IN accuracy minus OUT accuracy

rows.measure: Distribution of per-example counterfactual memorization scores
rows.value: The paper reports memorization in all three datasets; the distributions are shown in Figure 1.
rows.note: No numerical distribution values are stated in the text; counterfactual memorization is distinct from the listed generalization-gap measures.
rows.check: Counterfactual self-influence is measured, but no targeted-removal versus random-removal test of V8 is performed.

rows.subject: Transformer-based language models equivalent to (decoder only) T5-base
rows.operation_detail: Measured how counterfactual memorization changed over training epochs.
rows.measure: Fraction of examples with counterfactual memorization consistently above thresholds; trend across epochs
rows.value: About 59% of examples had consistently increasing memorization scores across all epochs considered; 0.5% never rose above 0.1; 85% never rose above 0.2. More training epochs significantly increases memorization.
rows.note: These are memorization dynamics, not a measurement of a listed version's generalization gap.
rows.check: The numbers match the text. These are memorization dynamics, not a listed version's effect.

rows.subject: Transformer-based language models equivalent to (decoder only) T5-base
rows.operation_detail: Compared each RealNews example's counterfactual memorization score with its number of near-duplicates.
rows.measure: Pearson correlation between counterfactual memorization and number of near-duplicates
rows.note: The paper describes an inverse correlation; this is not one of the listed claim-version measures.
rows.check: The -0.39 correlation applies only to approximately 38,000 examples having at least one near-duplicate, not the entire RealNews training set. It does not test V8's removal comparison.

rows.subject: Transformer-based language models equivalent to (decoder only) T5-base
rows.operation_detail: Estimated the maximum influence of each training example on validation-set examples using counterfactual influence.
rows.measure: Relationship between training-example counterfactual memorization and its maximum influence on any validation example
rows.value: Examples with small memorization scores have small maximum-influence scores; larger validation influence generally requires larger memorization, but maximum influence drops for memorization larger than 0.4.
rows.note: The reported association concerns prediction influence, not the claim versions' generalization gaps.
rows.check: The association is correctly reported but does not establish aggregate accuracy loss from targeted removal relative to random removal. Appendix Figure 6 also reports C4.

rows.subject: Grover-Mega (p=0.96)
rows.operation_detail: Estimated the maximum counterfactual influence of training examples on publicly released generated examples.
rows.measure: Maximum counterfactual influence on generated examples
rows.value: The influence histogram decays faster and its maximum-influence value range is twice smaller than for train-validation influence.
rows.note: Authors attribute the limited high-influence findings partly to the smaller generation sample and analysis restricted to the first 2M training examples.
rows.check: Grover-Mega supplies the generated texts; the counterfactual scoring uses the study's subset-trained language models, not retrained Grover-Mega models. Figure 10 takes the maximum over training examples for each generated example, rather than over generated examples for each training example. Correct the subject and maximum's direction.
